overview: Newhall Terrace Apartments is a 66-unit apartment building at 24377 Newhall Avenue in Santa Clarita, built in 1972 on a 2.14 acre parcel and containing approximately 36,908 gross square feet across two stories.

The property is a single floor plan asset. All 66 units are one bedroom, one bath homes of approximately 550 square feet, which makes the rent roll unusually simple to underwrite and unusually simple to manage: one unit type, one turn cost, one market rent to solve for.

Sixty of the 66 units are leased, and two of them are already at the $1,900 market rent carried in this analysis. The other 58 average $1,584. Across those 58 units the gap is roughly $220,000 of annual rent the property is not currently collecting, and no entitlement, construction, or repositioning is required to reach it. The $1,900 is not a projection borrowed from a comparable set: this building has leased units at it.

Because Santa Clarita has no local rent stabilization ordinance, the gap closes on turnover rather than through a capped annual increase. Seven units were vacant at the rent roll date, which means a portion of that repositioning is available to a buyer immediately rather than over a holding period.
properties.location_title: Walking Distance to Metrolink in Old Town Newhall
location_narrative: The property sits on Newhall Avenue at the edge of Old Town Newhall. Newhall Metrolink Station is three tenths of a mile away, a six minute walk, putting a tenant on a one seat rail ride to Burbank, Glendale, and Union Station without a car. The Oaks Plaza is two tenths of a mile from the door and the Newhall Crossings retail and residential development is three tenths of a mile.
William S. Hart Regional Park is a twelve minute walk. College of the Canyons is 4.8 miles out and Henry Mayo Newhall Hospital, one of the valley's largest employers, is 1.9 miles away.

This is the walkable end of the Santa Clarita Valley, which is uncommon in a market built overwhelmingly around the car. For a building of 550 square foot one bedrooms, a tenant base that can live here without a second vehicle is not a soft amenity, it is what supports the rent.
physical_narrative: Two stories, 66 units, approximately 36,908 gross square feet on a 93,152 square foot lot. The Los Angeles County Assessor records the property under APN 2830-017-015 as a Multi-Family Residence built in 1972, and the unit count, year built, building area, and lot size in this analysis all tie to that record.

Improvements sit across garden-style wings served by numbered covered carports along two interior runs, and by two on-site laundry rooms running Speed Queen commercial equipment. Every unit has air conditioning and heating.
Electrical service runs through Siemens panels.

That is worth stating plainly. On a Los Angeles County building of this vintage the first thing a buyer's inspector looks for is a Federal Pacific or Zinsco panel. Both are recognized fire hazards, both are awkward to insure around, and both normally end in a replacement credit off the purchase price. This property does not carry that problem.

Buyer demand here is real and it is currently deeper than the supply of listed product.

That demand is disciplined, not indiscriminate. An eight-unit building a fifth of a mile away has been marketed for eleven months without selling, at an ask well above where this submarket has actually been closing. Buyers here are active, and they are also willing to wait out a number they do not believe.

That combination is scarce in the Santa Clarita Valley, and it is the core of the positioning.

valuation_narrative: The recommendation rests on current income rather than on the pro forma. Closed arm's-length sales in Newhall run from $176,607 to $209,091 per unit, and the only closed trade at comparable scale, a 65-unit building half a mile up the same street, allocated at $182,692 per unit inside a four-property portfolio transaction. At $174,242 per unit the recommendation sits below all of them. Unit size is the reason.

This building averages 559 square feet per unit, the smallest in the comparable set. The closed sales run from 607 square feet a unit at 24810 Newhall Avenue up to 907 at 18046 Beneda Lane, so a buyer paying by the door gets less square footage here than at any of them. Price per square foot is where the two reconcile. At $311.59 the recommendation lands within three cents of 24810 Newhall Avenue at $311.56, the closest comparable on unit size and the only single-asset trade in the set. On current income it prices at a 6.08% capitalization rate and an 8.95 gross rent multiplier.

Two things move this number more than the comparables do. The first is the rent gap. In-place rents average $1,584 against a $1,900 market rent, 17% of upside measured across the whole building, on an asset with no local rent stabilization ordinance. The second is how the unleased units are carried. The vacant units, the manager unit and the two units the rent roll does not list sit in scheduled rent at the $1,900 market rent rather than at an achieved rent, which is standard practice for a marketed vacancy and is what the current capitalization rate is struck on. Ownership prices its current vacancies at $1,590 to $1,630. The sensitivity table prices that case, the owner's higher reported repairs and management, and the case where vacancy is carried at the 6.06% shown on the June rent roll rather than at the 3% lenders underwrite for turnover.

The property was originally developed with 1987 low-income housing tax credits. That allocation carried a fifteen-year compliance period and no extended-use covenant, since the thirty-year requirement arrived only for allocations after 1989, and the restrictions expired in 2002. Ownership confirms the property carries no rent restriction and no age restriction today. Third-party data services still display the historical allocation, which is a record of a 1987 program rather than a live covenant. It does explain the rent profile: rents were held down for fifteen years and were never reset to market afterward.

Stabilized at market rent with utility bill-back at $75 per unit per month, net operating income reaches $960,159. That figure is a projection of what the property can earn, not what it earns today, and the recommendation does not rest on it.

strategy.title: Lead With the Rent Gap, Not the Vacancy
strategy.copy: The single most valuable fact about this property is that the occupied units sit roughly 20% below where the one-bedroom market is. That is the cleanest story in this submarket and it is what the campaign leads with.

Newhall Terrace Apartments is a 66-unit apartment building at 24377 Newhall Avenue in Santa Clarita, built in 1972 on a 2.14 acre parcel and containing approximately 36,908 gross square feet across two stories.

The property is a single floor plan asset. All 66 units are one bedroom, one bath homes of approximately 550 square feet, which makes the rent roll unusually simple to underwrite and unusually simple to manage: one unit type, one turn cost, one market rent to solve for.

Sixty of the 66 units are leased, and two of them are already at the $1,900 market rent carried in this analysis. The other 58 average $1,584. Across those 58 units the gap is roughly $220,000 of annual rent the property is not currently collecting, and no entitlement, construction, or repositioning is required to reach it. The $1,900 is not a projection borrowed from a comparable set: this building has leased units at it.

Because Santa Clarita has no local rent stabilization ordinance, the gap closes on turnover rather than through a capped annual increase. Seven units were vacant at the rent roll date, which means a portion of that repositioning is available to a buyer immediately rather than over a holding period.
Walking Distance to Metrolink in Old Town Newhall

The property sits on Newhall Avenue at the edge of Old Town Newhall. Newhall Metrolink Station is three tenths of a mile away, a six minute walk, putting a tenant on a one seat rail ride to Burbank, Glendale, and Union Station without a car. The Oaks Plaza is two tenths of a mile from the door and the Newhall Crossings retail and residential development is three tenths of a mile.
William S. Hart Regional Park is a twelve minute walk. College of the Canyons is 4.8 miles out and Henry Mayo Newhall Hospital, one of the valley's largest employers, is 1.9 miles away.

This is the walkable end of the Santa Clarita Valley, which is uncommon in a market built overwhelmingly around the car. For a building of 550 square foot one bedrooms, a tenant base that can live here without a second vehicle is not a soft amenity, it is what supports the rent.

Two stories, 66 units, approximately 36,908 gross square feet on a 93,152 square foot lot. The Los Angeles County Assessor records the property under APN 2830-017-015 as a Multi-Family Residence built in 1972, and the unit count, year built, building area, and lot size in this analysis all tie to that record.

Improvements sit across garden-style wings served by numbered covered carports along two interior runs, and by two on-site laundry rooms running Speed Queen commercial equipment. Every unit has air conditioning and heating.
Electrical service runs through Siemens panels.

That is worth stating plainly. On a Los Angeles County building of this vintage the first thing a buyer's inspector looks for is a Federal Pacific or Zinsco panel. Both are recognized fire hazards, both are awkward to insure around, and both normally end in a replacement credit off the purchase price. This property does not carry that problem.
At 2.14 acres the parcel is generously sized for 66 units, roughly 31 units to the acre, with meaningful open and landscaped area rather than a building built to its lot lines.

The site is a single legal parcel assembled from lots 29, 30, 31 and 32 of Tract 1059 together with the adjoining vacated street, held in fee simple. It fronts Newhall Avenue between 9th Street and Chestnut Street.
Nearby leased and asking rents are shown as a market sensitivity for the one bedroom floor plan and are not represented as achieved subject rents.

The recommendation rests on current income rather than on the pro forma. Closed arm's-length sales in Newhall run from $176,607 to $209,091 per unit, and the only closed trade at comparable scale, a 65-unit building half a mile up the same street, allocated at $182,692 per unit inside a four-property portfolio transaction. At $174,242 per unit the recommendation sits below all of them. Unit size is the reason.

This building averages 559 square feet per unit, the smallest in the comparable set. The closed sales run from 607 square feet a unit at 24810 Newhall Avenue up to 907 at 18046 Beneda Lane, so a buyer paying by the door gets less square footage here than at any of them. Price per square foot is where the two reconcile. At $311.59 the recommendation lands within three cents of 24810 Newhall Avenue at $311.56, the closest comparable on unit size and the only single-asset trade in the set. On current income it prices at a 6.08% capitalization rate and an 8.95 gross rent multiplier.

Two things move this number more than the comparables do. The first is the rent gap. In-place rents average $1,584 against a $1,900 market rent, 17% of upside measured across the whole building, on an asset with no local rent stabilization ordinance. The second is how the unleased units are carried. The vacant units, the manager unit and the two units the rent roll does not list sit in scheduled rent at the $1,900 market rent rather than at an achieved rent, which is standard practice for a marketed vacancy and is what the current capitalization rate is struck on. Ownership prices its current vacancies at $1,590 to $1,630. The sensitivity table prices that case, the owner's higher reported repairs and management, and the case where vacancy is carried at the 6.06% shown on the June rent roll rather than at the 3% lenders underwrite for turnover.

The property was originally developed with 1987 low-income housing tax credits. That allocation carried a fifteen-year compliance period and no extended-use covenant, since the thirty-year requirement arrived only for allocations after 1989, and the restrictions expired in 2002. Ownership confirms the property carries no rent restriction and no age restriction today. Third-party data services still display the historical allocation, which is a record of a 1987 program rather than a live covenant. It does explain the rent profile: rents were held down for fifteen years and were never reset to market afterward.

claims.text: Stabilized at market rent with utility bill-back at $75 per unit per month, net operating income reaches $960,159. That figure is a projection of what the property can earn, not what it earns today, and the recommendation does not rest on it.

Operating figures are drawn from the supporting Marcus & Millichap model dated September 10, 2026 and from the owner's August 2026 operating summary. Current rents are taken from the seller's June 2026 rent roll, with the vacant, TBD and manager units carried at the $1,900 market rent. Real estate taxes are carried at a reassessed $181,415, being $136,402 of ad valorem at the county rate of 1.1861% for tax rate area 00223 plus $45,013 of direct assessments, which are flat charges that do not move with the sale price. Insurance, repairs and maintenance, contract services and management are carried at underwritten figures; the owner's summary reports higher repairs and management and lower insurance and gardening, and the sensitivity table prices the owner's case alongside the case where the unleased units are carried at the leased average instead. Proposed financing reflects the loan terms in the supporting model and is subject to change; a buyer should obtain its own terms.

Four of the closed sales shown closed together as a single four-property portfolio transaction on June 23, 2026, and their individual prices are allocations within that transaction rather than four independent trades. Each of the four carries its own recorded loan at 75% of its allocated price, so a lender underwrote every allocation on its own. The LAAA Team's own assignments in this market appear in the Track Record and are not used as comparables.

rent_control.conclusion: The property sits in the City of Santa Clarita, which has no local rent stabilization ordinance and no local just-cause ordinance. A 1972 building is therefore governed by the statewide Tenant Protection Act (AB 1482), which caps annual increases at 5% plus CPI to a 10% ceiling and permits a reset to market rent on voluntary turnover.

exceptions.description: CoStar tags the subject Market Segment Senior, Rent Type Affordable, Affordable Type Rent Restricted, Affordable Units 66. This traces to a real primary record: HUD LIHTC database entry CAA00000007, state ID CA-87-033, 24377 NEWHALL AVE, SANTA CLARITA, 66 total and 66 low-income units, tax credits allocated 1987. ZIP+4 91321-2726 and coordinates 34.3786 / -118.531778 match APN 2830-017-015. The property WAS a 1987 Low-Income Housing Tax Credit deal. The restrictions have since lapsed: a 1987 allocation carries a 15-year compliance period and no extended-use covenant, because the 30-year requirement added by OBRA 1989 does not reach pre-1990 allocations. Logan Ward confirmed directly with ownership on 2026-09-04 that there is no LIHTC restriction and no senior restriction on the property now, and that the restriction fell off in 2002. That is consistent with every other fact on file: the City of Santa Clarita affordable rental housing list does not include the property, the assessor records Exemption None with an individual owner, the September 2006 sale to individuals for $6,250,000 came just after a 1987 compliance period would have run out, and in-place rents spread from $1,425 to $1,880 rather than sitting on an AMI schedule. The property is therefore underwritten and marketed as unrestricted market-rate housing, and the HUD database entry is a historical allocation record rather than a live covenant. ADDITIONAL FINDING 2026-09-09: the property's own live listings on after55.com and apartments.com carry the line 'This property is intended and operated in accordance with the Housing for Older Persons provisions of the Fair Housing Act', which is consistent with CoStar's Senior market-segment tag. Housing for Older Persons is a voluntary Fair Housing Act election by an owner, not a recorded covenant, so it does not contradict clear title. Logan Ward reaffirmed on 2026-09-09 that there is no senior and no affordable component, that the deed restriction lifted in the early 2000s, and that the property is a regular market-rate apartment building. Nothing about senior housing is published. The portal flags appear to be stale marketing left from the LIHTC era and are flagged to ownership for removal.
